messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Nathan is a 33-year-old prosecutor in a Midwestern district attorney's office, married for six years to a high school teacher. He had been leading a high-profile terrorism-related trial when a bomb detonated in the courthouse parking garage. He escaped with minor injuries, but two colleagues and a security guard were killed. In the aftermath, Nathan could not hold a coherent sequence of the minutes before and after the blast. What he carried instead were fragments—the pressure wave, the silence afterward, the smell of gasoline and burnt rubber. That smell, or anything that remotely resembles it, still pulls him back as though no time has passed. The memory feels more real than ordinary recollections; it has a vivid, present-tense quality that leaves him disoriented, as if he is still standing in the smoke.

Nathan works long hours, often arriving home exhausted. Fatigue now functions as a trigger: when he is drained, the intrusive images surface more easily, and with them comes a wave of self-condemnation. He cannot forgive himself for not doing more, for not warning people fast enough. In his darker moments he is certain he should have protected others and failed. These appraisals tighten around him when he encounters any reminder. A colleague’s cologne that carries a hint of alcohol sets off the same loop: the scent appears, and within seconds Nathan is mentally back in the garage, replaying his inaction. He has begun avoiding after-work social events where drinks are served, telling his wife he is too tired. The exhaustion itself then becomes another reminder of his perceived weakness, feeding the guilt.

His guilt, in turn, deepens the fragmentation of his memory. The more he blames himself, the more the event feels present rather than past, as though he must keep reliving it to find a way to change the outcome. Yet the story remains stubbornly incoherent; he cannot piece together why he survived when others did not. This lack of narrative fuels his distrust of people around him. He catches himself scrutinizing colleagues’ motives, wondering if they are hiding something. At work he avoids the parking garage and takes a longer route through the building, even though he knows the explosion was a one-time event. He has started leaving his office early to avoid the echo of footsteps in the hallway, which can sound like running before a blast.

The memory itself also triggers his physical state. When a spontaneous image of the explosion surfaces—often when he is tired or hears a sudden bang—his heart pounds and he feels the fatigue deepen, as though the recollection drains him. The tiredness then becomes another cue. This cycle has eroded his concentration; he has missed filing deadlines and received a formal warning from his supervisor. At home he is irritable, and his wife has commented that he seems “somewhere else.” What finally brought Nathan to seek help was a moment in court: a door slammed, he flinched, and he realized he had been scanning the room for exits. He is afraid that if he does not get control of this, he will lose his career and his marriage. But what frightens him most is the thought that facing the memories will only prove that he really did fail.
